results.description: At each outer iteration t, agent j generates a random permutation π_t = (π_t^0, …, π_t^{n-1}) of {1,…,n} uniformly without replacement.
results.evidence: src/algorithms.py line 100: `order = rng.permutation(n_local)` is called inside the outer epoch loop (line 93: `for epoch in range(epochs)`) and the per-agent loop (line 96: `for j in range(agents)`), specifically under the `dpg_rr` branch (random reshuffling). `rng.permutation(n_local)` produces a uniform random permutation of {0, ..., n_local-1} (the local dataset indices) without replacement — exactly matching π_t for each agent j at each outer iteration t.
results.note: The permutation is zero-indexed in code vs. 1-indexed in the paper, but this is equivalent. The method is named `dpg_rr` (distributed proximal gradient with random reshuffling), consistent with Algorithm 1 in the paper.

results.description: For i = 0,…,n-1, agent j updates x_{j,t}^{i+1} = x_{j,t}^i - γ ∇ f_{j,π_t^i}(x_{j,t}^i), where γ is a constant step-size.
results.evidence: src/algorithms.py lines 94–109: for the dpg_rr/dpg_sg/dpg_ig methods, each agent j initializes w = x_agents[:, j].copy() then loops over indices with `w -= step_size * _sample_gradient(local_x[j][idx], local_y[j][idx], w)`. This is exactly x_{j,t}^{i+1} = x_{j,t}^i - γ ∇f_{j,π_t^i}(x_{j,t}^i), where step_size (γ) is the constant step-size passed in or defaulted at lines 80–81. The iteration variable idx plays the role of π_t^i, the local sample index in inner loop iteration i.
results.note: The update is implemented as in-place subtraction `w -= step_size * grad` which is equivalent to the stated formula. All three variants (RR, SG, IG) share this same update rule, differing only in how the order array is constructed.

results.description: After the inner loop, agent j computes v_{j,t} via a multi-step consensus mapping: v_{j,t} = ∑_{l=1}^m λ_{jl,t} x_{l,t}^n, where λ_{jl,t} is the (j,l)-th entry of the transition matrix Φ(T(t)+t, T(t)), Φ(k,τ) = A(k)⋯A(τ), and A(t) is the doubly stochastic adjacency matrix at time t. The number of communication steps performed at iteration t is exactly t.
results.evidence: src/algorithms.py, function `_mix` (lines ~37–44): builds transition matrix `p = A(steps) @ ... @ A(1)` where `steps = epoch + 1` (i.e., exactly t communication steps at 0-indexed epoch t-1), then returns `q @ p.T`, which computes for each agent j the weighted sum `∑_l p[l,j] * q[:,l]` — matching v_{j,t} = ∑_l λ_{jl,t} x_{l,t}^n. The transition matrix is the product of t doubly-stochastic adjacency matrices A(t)⋯A(1) = Φ(T(t)+t, T(t)). Called after the inner loop for DPG-RR/SG/IG: `mixed = _mix(q, networks, epoch, time_varying)` where `q[:,j]` holds the post-inner-loop iterate x_{j,t}^n.
results.note: The epoch variable is 0-indexed, so at epoch=0 we get 1 communication step, at epoch=1 we get 2, etc. — this matches "exactly t communication steps at iteration t" for t=1,2,3,...

results.description: The consensus mapping is implemented by performing t communication rounds: at each round, agent j sends its current estimate to neighbors, receives their estimates, and updates as a weighted average using the entries of the adjacency matrix A at that communication time step.
results.evidence: src/algorithms.py, function `_mix` (lines ~35-43): performs `steps = epoch + 1` communication rounds in a loop. At each round `s`, it selects the adjacency matrix `a = networks[s % len(networks)]` (time-varying) or `networks[0]` (fixed), and accumulates the product `p = a @ p`. The final return `q @ p.T` gives the weighted-average consensus update. This exactly matches t rounds of consensus with the adjacency matrix A at each communication time step.
results.note: The `steps` count is `epoch + 1`, so t grows with each epoch (matching the paper's Section III description of t-step consensus maps). The time-varying path selects a different A at each round using modular indexing over the `networks` list.

results.description: Agent j then applies the proximal operator: x_{j,t+1} = prox_{γ,φ}(v_{j,t}), where prox_{α,h}(x) = argmin_y { h(y) + (1/(2α))‖y - x‖^2 }.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py, the proximal operator is implemented as `_soft_threshold(v, threshold)` (line ~30): `np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - threshold, 0.0)`, which is the closed-form prox for the L1 regularizer φ = λ‖·‖₁. This is applied after the consensus mixing step for the main DPG methods: `x_agents = _soft_threshold(mixed, step_size * lam)` (line ~82), directly implementing x_{j,t+1} = prox_{γ,φ}(v_{j,t}) where v_{j,t} = mixed is the result of the consensus mixing step and γ = step_size, φ = lam‖·‖₁. The same pattern appears in prox_g/prox_g_rr and `next` methods as well.
results.note: The proximal operator is specialized to the L1 norm (soft thresholding), consistent with the paper's use of φ as the L1 regularizer. The general form prox_{α,h}(x) = argmin_y { h(y) + (1/(2α))‖y-x‖² } is implemented implicitly via its closed-form solution for h = λ‖·‖₁.

results.description: The proximal operator is evaluated exactly once per outer iteration (epoch), not after each inner gradient step.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py, the `dpg_rr`/`dpg_sg`/`dpg_ig` branch (lines ~75-86) implements an inner loop (`for idx in order: w -= step_size * _sample_gradient(...)`) with no proximal call inside it. The soft-thresholding proximal operator (`_soft_threshold(mixed, step_size * lam)`) is called exactly once per epoch, outside the inner loop, after all n local gradient steps and after the consensus mixing step (`_mix`). This confirms the proximal operator is applied once per outer iteration (epoch), not after each inner gradient step.
results.note: The same once-per-epoch proximal pattern also holds for the `prox_g`/`prox_g_rr` and `next` baseline methods, but the key claim concerns the main DPG-RR/SG/IG algorithms from Algorithm 1 (Remark III.2).

results.description: The step-size γ is held constant across all outer iterations; the algorithm does not use a diminishing step-size sequence.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py, step_size is set once before the epoch loop (lines 80-81) and used as a constant in the DPG methods (dpg_rr, dpg_sg, dpg_ig) throughout all outer iterations. Line 106: `w -= step_size * _sample_gradient(...)` and line 109: `x_agents = _soft_threshold(mixed, step_size * lam)` both use the same unchanged step_size at every epoch. The epoch loop (lines 93-165) has no update to step_size for these methods. By contrast, baseline methods like DGM (line 120: `step_size / np.sqrt(epoch + 1.0)`) and NEXT (line 155: `step_size / (epoch + 1.0) ** 0.6`) explicitly use diminishing step-sizes, confirming the DPG methods intentionally use constant γ.
results.note: The constant step-size is the paper's Algorithm 1 design. The code correctly distinguishes DPG methods (constant step) from baseline methods that may use diminishing steps.

results.description: The gradient ∇ f_{j,π_t^i}(x_{j,t}^i) is computed at the current inner iterate x_{j,t}^i, not at the start-of-epoch point x_{j,t}.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py lines 96–107, the DPG-RR/SG/IG inner loop initializes `w = x_agents[:, j].copy()` (the start-of-epoch point) and then iterates: `w -= step_size * _sample_gradient(local_x[j][idx], local_y[j][idx], w)`. The gradient `_sample_gradient(...)` receives `w` as its third argument — the *current* (mutated) inner iterate — not the original `x_agents[:, j]`. Because `w` is updated in-place before the next call, each gradient is evaluated at the running inner iterate `x_{j,t}^i`, matching Eq. (7) / Algorithm 1 line 8.
results.note: All three variants (dpg_rr, dpg_sg, dpg_ig) share this same inner loop structure.

results.description: Each agent j initializes its local variable x_{j,0} arbitrarily before the first iteration.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py, the initial state of all agents is set at line: `x_agents = np.ones((d, agents), dtype=np.float64) if init == "ones" else np.zeros((d, agents), dtype=np.float64)`. The `init` parameter defaults to "ones", and run_experiment.py calls `run_method` without specifying `init`, so all experiments use all-ones initialization. No random or arbitrary per-agent initialization is implemented. There is no code path where x_{j,0} is set to an arbitrary (e.g., random) value per agent.
results.note: The paper's Algorithm 1 line 2 states agents initialize x_{j,0} arbitrarily, but the code enforces a fixed deterministic initialization (all-ones by default, or all-zeros). Equivalent-but-different does not apply here since fixed initialization is a strict subset of "arbitrary."

results.description: GT-SAGA and DSGD use subgradients instead of gradients because the cost function is non-smooth.
results.evidence: In src/algorithms.py: DSGD (lines 118-125) computes `q[:, j] = x_agents[:, j] - alpha * (g + lam * np.sign(x_agents[:, j]))` — the subgradient of the L1 norm (`np.sign(...)`) is added directly to the stochastic gradient. GT-SAGA (lines 127-144) computes `g_est = g_now - g_old + saga_means[j] + lam * np.sign(w)` — again the L1 subgradient is folded into the gradient estimate. Neither method uses a proximal operator; instead both handle the non-smooth L1 regularizer via its subgradient `np.sign`. In contrast, NEXT explicitly uses `_soft_threshold` (a proximal operator) and comments that "the nonsmooth L1 term is handled by the single prox below; it is not included in the tracked smooth gradient." (lines 148-156).
results.note: The non-smooth cost is an L1-regularized logistic regression objective. The sign function (`np.sign`) is a standard subgradient of the L1 norm, confirming the claim that GT-SAGA and DSGD use subgradients rather than gradients (or proximal operators) to handle the non-smooth term.

Both `dpg_rr` (lines using `step_size` in the RR inner loop and soft_threshold call) and `prox_g` (line using `step_size * g` and soft_threshold) use the same constant `step_size` without any epoch-dependent scaling. The config.json files for time_varying experiments confirm a single `step_size` field: `0.3` for w8a and `0.2` for a9a — applied uniformly to all methods including DPG-RR and Prox-G. run_experiment.py also confirms a single `--step-size` argument shared across all methods in a profile.

results.description: NEXT uses diminishing step-sizes.

results.description: DGM uses diminishing step-sizes.

The time_varying experiment config (results/formal/time_varying_w8a_seed0/config.json) confirms that DGM is one of the methods run in the `experiment: "time_varying"` setup.
results.note: The diminishing schedule is 1/sqrt(t), a standard choice for non-smooth stochastic optimization.
